    Compromised Injective SDK npm Package Exfiltrates Wallet Keys and Mnemonics
    socket.dev · 09 Jul 2026 13:32 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
    TAGSgithubgithub-account-compromiseinjective-labsinjective-tsinjectivelabs-sdk-tsinjectivelabs-wallet-coreinjectivelabs-wallet-cosmosinjectivelabs-wallet-evminjectivelabs-wallet-private-keymnemonic-exfiltrationnpmprivate-key-exfiltrationsocketsoftware-supply-chain-compromise
    In plain words

    A version of Injective Labs’ software package for JavaScript developers was altered so that, when people used it to create or load crypto wallets, it secretly sent away the words or codes needed to control those wallets. Developers and apps using version 1.20.21 of this package, or 17 related Injective Labs packages that pointed to it, could have exposed users’ wallet access information. This matters because those words and codes are enough for someone else to recreate the wallet and take any crypto assets in it, though the bad version was noticed and replaced quickly.

    Summary
    A compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts npm release, version 1.20.21, secretly exfiltrated wallet mnemonics and private keys during normal SDK use, with 17 related @injectivelabs packages also pinned to the malicious version. Anyone who used these versions should upgrade to a clean release and treat any exposed keys or seed phrases as compromised.

    Socket detected a malicious @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 release on npm that used fake telemetry functionality to exfiltrate wallet private keys and mnemonic phrases. The affected package is part of the Injective Labs TypeScript SDK and receives roughly 50,000 weekly downloads. The malicious functionality was introduced through commits from a GitHub account belonging to a developer with an established contribution history in the repository.

    The impact extended beyond direct users of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts because version 1.20.21 was also published across 17 additional @injectivelabs scoped packages. Those packages depended on and pinned the malicious SDK version, exposing users who may not have installed the SDK directly. The compromised version was deprecated on npm but had not been removed at the time of writing, and related GitHub release artifacts were still present.

    The malicious code was located in /dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js and /dist/cjs/accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs, where the fromMnemonic and fromHex functions were hooked to call trackKeyDerivation. That function recorded the method used and the sensitive information needed to derive the key, then base64-encoded and sent the records through a POST request to https://testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network. The article advises developers to move to clean version 1.20.23, audit direct and transitive dependencies, and treat any private key or mnemonic passed through the affected packages as compromised.

    • Because the malicious code ran during normal wallet functions rather than at install time, projects could install the package without immediately triggering the theft behavior.
    • The exfiltration endpoint was an Injective Labs public infrastructure endpoint, which made the malicious network traffic appear similar to ordinary Injective software traffic.
    • Deprecation on npm did not remove the malicious version, so it remained downloadable even after being marked as compromised.
    • Auditing only direct dependencies is insufficient because the attacker published related @injectivelabs packages that pinned the compromised SDK version as a dependency.
    • The article states the malicious version had 310 downloads, suggesting the real-world impact was much smaller than the potential exposure from a package with about 50,000 weekly downloads.
    Key Points
    • 01Socket detected a malicious @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 npm release that exfiltrated wallet private keys and mnemonic phrases through fake telemetry functionality.
    • 02The malicious code was introduced through commits from a GitHub account belonging to an established Injective Labs repository contributor, with suspicious activity starting on June 8, 2026.
    • 03The threat actor also published version 1.20.21 across 17 additional @injectivelabs scoped packages that depended on and pinned the malicious SDK version, exposing transitive users.
    • 04The malicious functionality hooked the fromMnemonic and fromHex functions and sent base64-encoded key material through a POST request to https://testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.
    • 05Developers are advised to move to clean version 1.20.23, audit direct and transitive @injectivelabs dependencies, and treat any private key or mnemonic phrase passed through the affected packages as compromised.
    OPEN SOURCE ↗
    JUSTIFICATION

    This is a specific supply-chain compromise of a popular npm package used in crypto wallet workflows, with malicious code capable of exfiltrating private keys and mnemonic phrases. It has broad relevance for security professionals because 17 related packages pinned the malicious version and any exposed wallet secrets must be treated as compromised, though the article states the issue was detected and contained relatively quickly.

    In plain words

    A bad release of an Injective software package on npm secretly copied people’s wallet seed phrases and private keys when apps used it, then sent them to an attacker-controlled web address disguised as normal Injective traffic. People and projects that installed @injectivelabs/sdk-ts version 1.20.21, or one of 17 related @injectivelabs packages that pulled it in, are affected. This matters because anyone whose wallet secret passed through the package should assume it was exposed, move their funds, and replace the keys and seed phrases.

    Summary
    A malicious npm release of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 stole wallet mnemonics and private keys during normal key derivation and exfiltrated them as fake gRPC telemetry. Anyone who used the affected Injective packages should upgrade to 1.20.23 and treat any exposed keys or seed phrases as compromised.

    A malicious release of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts, version 1.20.21, shipped code that recorded wallet mnemonics and private keys as they were derived and sent them to an attacker-controlled endpoint. The package receives around 50,000 weekly downloads, and the bad version was live on npm for under an hour on June 8, 2026. During that window, the attacker also republished the same version number across 17 other packages in the @injectivelabs scope, each pinned to the poisoned SDK.

    The stealer did not run at install time or break SDK behavior, but instead waited until an application called normal wallet key-derivation functions. It hooked PrivateKey.fromMnemonic and PrivateKey.fromHex, capturing full seed phrases or raw private keys before legitimate derivation continued. The stolen data was queued, base64-encoded, and sent in the X-Request-Id header to https://testnet[.]archival[.]chain[.]grpc-web[.]injective[.]network/, using gRPC-web-looking headers to blend in with normal Injective traffic.

    The malicious version was downloaded 310 times before it was pulled, and the maintainer published a clean version, 1.20.23, shortly after reverting the change. The article says the compromise appears to have come through commits from an established GitHub account, pointing to account takeover rather than a drive-by. Any mnemonic or private key that passed through the affected packages should be treated as exposed, with users advised to move funds, rotate keys and seed phrases, and upgrade affected @injectivelabs packages to 1.20.23.

    • Install-time scanners and sandboxes that only monitor package lifecycle scripts could miss this compromise because the stealer did not run during installation and only activated when an application derived a wallet key during normal use.
    • Auditing only direct dependencies is insufficient in this incident because 17 related @injectivelabs packages were republished to pin the poisoned SDK as a transitive dependency.
    • The exfiltration was designed to blend into legitimate Injective application traffic by using a lookalike gRPC-web endpoint, the application/grpc-web+proto content type, and the X-Request-Id header instead of the request body.
    • The malicious code was limited to two build artifacts and differed from the clean build by one injected block and two hook lines, showing how a small change in release artifacts can create severe wallet compromise.
    • Deprecation alone did not fully contain the risk because the article says the malicious npm version remained downloadable and compromised GitHub release artifacts were still present at the time of the source report.
    Key Points
    • 01A malicious release of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts version 1.20.21 recorded wallet mnemonics and private keys during key derivation and sent them to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
    • 02The malicious package was live on npm for under an hour on June 8, 2026, before the maintainer noticed and published a clean fix.
    • 03The attacker also republished 17 other @injectivelabs packages at version 1.20.21 with hard dependency pins to the poisoned sdk-ts package, causing projects using those packages to pull it transitively.
    • 04The stealer disguised its exfiltration as gRPC-web telemetry by sending base64-encoded stolen data in the X-Request-Id header to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.
    • 05Any mnemonic or private key that passed through the affected packages should be treated as exposed, and users are advised to move funds, rotate keys and seed phrases, and upgrade affected @injectivelabs packages to version 1.20.23.
    OPEN SOURCE ↗
    JUSTIFICATION

    This is a specific software supply-chain compromise in a widely used npm package that directly exfiltrated wallet mnemonics and private keys, with transitive exposure through 17 related packages. It is highly actionable for security professionals because the article includes affected versions, indicators of compromise, technical behavior, and remediation steps, though the short exposure window and reported 310 downloads keep it below the highest urgency tier.

    Injective SDK on npm infected with cryptocurrency wallet stealer
    bleepingcomputer.com · 09 Jul 2026 20:10 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5

    In plain words

    Hackers took over a legitimate contributor’s GitHub account for Injective Labs and used it to publish a tainted version of software that developers use to build apps on the Injective blockchain. When developers used certain wallet-related features, the tainted software copied the secret words and private keys that control cryptocurrency wallets and sent them out disguised as normal traffic. Developers building wallets, trading tools, exchanges, finance apps, and payment tools may be affected, and the real-world risk is that attackers could use those secrets to move victims’ digital money to wallets they control.

    Summary
    Hackers compromised Injective Labs’ GitHub repository and published malicious npm packages that stole crypto wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when developers used wallet key functions. A clean version has been released, but anyone who installed the malicious 1.20.21 package should move funds to new wallets and rotate secrets.

    Hackers compromised the Injective Labs SDK project’s GitHub repository and used it to publish a malicious version of the @injectivelabs/sdk-ts package on npm. The affected version, 1.20.21, stole cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases. Socket, Ox Security, and StepSecurity detected the supply-chain attack, and Socket reported that the malicious version was downloaded 310 times before it was deprecated.

    Injective SDK is a TypeScript/JavaScript software development kit for building applications on the Injective blockchain. The package has 50,000 weekly npm downloads and is used by developers building cryptocurrency wallets, trading bots, decentralized exchanges, DeFi applications, and payment tools. The attacker also published version 1.20.21 for another 17 project-associated packages, pinning all of them to the compromised SDK version.

    The malware activated when developers used SDK functions that generate or import wallet keys, rather than when the package was installed. It captured full mnemonic seed phrases and private keys, encoded the data in base64, queued multiple keys and mnemonics for two seconds, and sent them in an HTTP POST request header to an Injective Labs public infrastructure endpoint. The legitimate account owner reverted the changes within minutes and published a clean release, version 1.20.23, and developers who suspect compromise are advised to transfer cryptocurrency to new wallets and rotate all secrets in their environment.

    • The malicious code did not run at installation time, so checking only install scripts would not be enough to detect this compromise.
    • The stolen wallet data was sent to an Injective Labs public infrastructure endpoint, making the outbound traffic appear legitimate.
    • The malware queued multiple keys and mnemonics for two seconds and bundled them into an HTTP request header before sending them.
    • Although the malicious npm version was deprecated, Socket reported that it was not removed and the malicious GitHub release artifacts remained available.
    Key Points
    • 01Hackers compromised a GitHub account belonging to a legitimate Injective Labs SDK project contributor and used it to publish malicious version 1.20.21 of the @injectivelabs/sdk-ts npm package.
    • 02The malicious package stole cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when developers used SDK functions that generate or import wallet keys.
    • 03The attacker also published version 1.20.21 for 17 other packages associated with the project, pinning all of them to the compromised SDK version.
    • 04Socket reported that the malicious package version was downloaded 310 times before it was deprecated, and Ox Security reported that 87 dependent packages had a cumulative download count of just over 112,000.
    • 05Developers who suspect compromise are advised to transfer their cryptocurrency to new wallets and rotate all secrets in their environment.

    JUSTIFICATION

    This is a specific npm supply-chain compromise affecting a widely used cryptocurrency SDK with 50,000 weekly downloads and multiple dependent packages. It is important for security professionals because the malicious package stole wallet private keys and seed phrases and may have compromised developer systems that fetched or used version 1.20.21.

In plain words

Attackers used access to a trusted Injective Labs developer’s account to publish poisoned versions of 18 software packages used by apps that work with the Injective blockchain. The hidden code copied wallet recovery phrases and private keys when wallets were created or loaded, then sent them to a server controlled by the attackers. Anyone whose application installed the affected 1.20.21 packages during that short window, or later used a cached copy, should assume any wallet secrets handled by that app were exposed. This matters because those secrets can let someone take control of crypto wallets and move funds.

Summary
Attackers compromised a trusted Injective Labs developer account and published backdoored npm packages that stole wallet seed phrases and private keys during wallet creation or loading. Anyone who installed the affected 1.20.21 packages should treat touched wallet secrets as exposed and rotate funds to new wallets.

On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer’s account to add a backdoor to Injective Labs’ official TypeScript SDK for the Injective blockchain. The malicious version, 1.20.21, was published across 18 related @injectivelabs npm packages and remained live for less than an hour before being pulled and fixed. Applications that installed any affected package during that window, or later used a cached copy, should treat any wallet secrets handled by those packages as exposed.

The backdoor was disguised as harmless key-derivation telemetry and was placed directly in PrivateKey.fromMnemonic() and PrivateKey.fromHex(), the SDK entry points for turning wallet recovery phrases or raw private keys into signing keys. When those functions were called, the code captured the mnemonic or private key, batched the data briefly, base64-encoded it, and sent it to https://testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network/. The data was carried in the X-Request-Id request header with an empty body and a Content-Type meant to resemble legitimate gRPC-Web traffic.

The article says the malicious release came through the repository’s own GitHub Actions trusted-publishing workflow, with provenance pointing to a commit on master authored under the existing maintainer identity thomasRalee. The 17 non-sdk-ts packages did not contain the payload themselves, but they pinned the exact backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 dependency. A later revert removed the telemetry file and call sites, and clean version 1.20.23 was published across all 18 affected packages.

  • The attack did not require a stolen npm token because the malicious packages were published through the repository’s own GitHub Actions trusted-publishing workflow after code was pushed to master.
  • The exfiltration endpoint was hidden as a character-code array and made to resemble legitimate Injective gRPC-Web infrastructure, which would make simple source searches for URLs less effective.
  • The stolen wallet secrets were sent in the X-Request-Id header with an empty body, so defenders would need to inspect headers in egress or proxy logs rather than only request bodies.
  • The 17 related packages did not contain the payload themselves but still created exposure because they pinned the exact malicious @injectivelabs/sdk-ts version.
  • Because the malicious code ran only when wallet keys were created or loaded, affected users must treat any wallet secrets touched by applications using the tainted package as exposed, not merely remove the package.
Key Points
  • 01On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to add a backdoor to Injective Labs' TypeScript SDK for the Injective blockchain.
  • 02The malicious code was disguised as key derivation telemetry and sent wallet recovery phrases or raw private keys to an attacker-controlled server when PrivateKey.fromMnemonic() or PrivateKey.fromHex() was called.
  • 03The malicious version 1.20.21 was published across 18 @injectivelabs packages, with 17 packages carrying risk because they pinned the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts dependency exactly.
  • 04The npm provenance for the malicious release pointed to a GitHub Actions trusted-publishing workflow from the InjectiveLabs/injective-ts repository, and the commits were authored under the existing maintainer identity thomasRalee.
  • 05Injective Labs removed the payload, deprecated version 1.20.21, and republished clean version 1.20.23 across all 18 affected packages about 49 minutes after the malicious packages went live.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a must-read because it reports a specific npm supply-chain compromise of Injective Labs packages that directly exposed crypto wallet seed phrases and private keys. The attack used a trusted maintainer account and the project’s own publishing pipeline, affected 18 packages, and requires impacted users to treat wallet secrets as compromised.

In plain words

AssuranceAmerica, a U.S. insurance company, says attackers got into its company systems and copied files containing information on 6,998,886 people. The people affected are drivers whose records may include names, contact details, insurance policy or account information, vehicle and claims information, and driver’s license numbers. This matters because that kind of personal information can put people at risk of suspicious financial activity, so the company is telling affected customers to watch their credit reports, bank accounts, and other financial statements.

Summary
AssuranceAmerica disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 7 million drivers after attackers accessed its IT systems and stole files containing personal, policy, vehicle, claims, and driver’s license information. The company says it has contained the intrusion, strengthened security measures, and is notifying affected individuals.

AssuranceAmerica disclosed a data breach affecting 6,998,886 people after attackers gained access to its systems earlier this year. The American insurance company provides auto, renters, and commercial auto insurance across 14 U.S. states through more than 9,500 independent agents. The breach was revealed in a filing with Maine’s Office of the Attorney General, though the company had not yet published a press release about the incident.

AssuranceAmerica detected suspicious activity on March 17, 2026, and said the activity appeared to result from malicious activity on March 16, 2026, that targeted one of its employees. The company determined that an unauthorized third party accessed certain portions of its IT environment and copied certain data files. Its review of the affected files was completed on June 15, 2026, and notification letters were scheduled to be sent to affected people on Friday.

The stolen documents contained combinations of names, contact information, automobile insurance policy or account information, driver or vehicle information, claims-related information, and driver’s license numbers. AssuranceAmerica said it disabled compromised credentials, ended unauthorized sessions, isolated affected systems, notified law enforcement, reset passwords, deployed enhanced monitoring and threat detection tools, and provided additional cybersecurity instruction to personnel. The company advised affected customers to review credit reports, bank accounts, and other financial statements, and to alert their financial institution if they detect suspicious activity.

  • A single targeted incident involving one employee led to exposure of records for nearly 7 million people, showing the scale of data accessible from the affected company systems.
  • The breach was detected on March 17, 2026, but AssuranceAmerica said notice is being sent only after the file review was completed on June 15, 2026, indicating that determining whose information was affected took about three months.
  • The incident became public through a filing with Maine's Office of the Attorney General even though AssuranceAmerica had not yet published a press release about it.
  • The stolen files combined identity, contact, insurance, vehicle, claims, and driver's license information, giving affected people multiple types of records to monitor for suspicious activity.
Key Points
  • 01AssuranceAmerica disclosed in a filing with Maine's Office of the Attorney General that a data breach exposed information belonging to 6,998,886 people.
  • 02AssuranceAmerica detected suspicious activity on March 17, 2026, and determined that malicious activity on March 16, 2026 targeted one of its employees.
  • 03The company said an unauthorized third party accessed parts of its IT environment and copied certain data files.
  • 04The stolen documents contained combinations of names, contact information, automobile insurance policy or account information, driver or vehicle information, claims-related information, and driver's license numbers.
  • 05AssuranceAmerica said it disabled compromised credentials and unauthorized sessions, isolated affected systems, notified law enforcement, reset passwords, deployed enhanced monitoring and threat detection tools, and provided additional cybersecurity instruction to personnel.

In plain words

Researchers found that a China-based group called Lurking Lizard has been using fake 7-Zip installers, lookalike websites, and other fake apps or services to secretly turn people’s computers into relay points for someone else’s internet traffic. Home users who download these fake tools are affected, and the article says similar schemes have also involved devices like smart TVs and streaming boxes. This matters because a person’s home internet address can then be used for hacking or other unauthorized activity, which can make their normal online activity look suspicious or get blocked.

Summary
Researchers say a China-based actor dubbed Lurking Lizard has used fake 7-Zip installers, lookalike domains, and other branded lures to turn victims’ devices into residential proxy nodes. The operation appears to be a full proxy-for-profit ecosystem, from infecting devices to marketing and selling access through fake proxy brands and review sites.

Cybersecurity researchers disclosed details of a threat actor dubbed Lurking Lizard that has operated an end-to-end malicious residential proxy business using more than 230 lookalike domains. Infoblox says the activity dates back to at least August 2022. One campaign observed earlier this year used a trojanized 7-Zip installer hosted on 7zip[.]com to covertly recruit compromised devices as proxy nodes.

Lurking Lizard has impersonated major proxy providers including IPIDEA, SmartProxy, IP Royal, and 911Proxy, and has also run fake independent review sites to drive traffic to its scam storefronts. WHOIS analysis and infrastructure fingerprinting suggest the actor is based in China. The operation also used popular VPNs and services like HeroSMS as decoys to distribute proxy malware.

The campaign evolved to use WireVPN branding and target users across Android, macOS, and Windows, including an Android app called “wirevpn - Fast Unlimited Proxy” that has more than 1 million downloads. The article says it is unclear whether the same proxy-node functionality is present in the mobile applications or limited to desktop applications. The broader impact is that compromised home devices can be used to funnel unauthorized third-party traffic, creating risks for device owners whose home IP addresses may be associated with suspicious or blocked activity.

  • Lurking Lizard’s use of drop-catching means expired domains with existing reputation can become distribution points for malicious installers, making domain history itself a potential trust risk.
  • The actor benefited from user confusion around a commonly mistyped or incorrectly referenced domain, using 7zip[.]com instead of the legitimate 7-zip[.]org to lure victims.
  • A single embedded IPLogger URL tied the 7-Zip campaign to fake installers for multiple brands, showing that small tracking artifacts can reveal shared infrastructure across otherwise separate-looking campaigns.
  • The operation did not stop at infecting devices; it also included fake proxy brands and fake independent review sites, indicating that the actor managed both victim acquisition and customer-facing monetization.
  • Proxyway found that 773,087 SmartProxy-linked IP addresses overlapped with a public IPIDEA dataset, suggesting infrastructure relationships between proxy services can expose connections in the residential proxy ecosystem.
Key Points
  • 01Researchers disclosed a threat actor dubbed Lurking Lizard that has operated an end-to-end malicious residential proxy business using more than 230 lookalike domains.
  • 02A campaign observed earlier this year used a trojanized 7-Zip installer hosted on 7zip[.]com to covertly recruit compromised devices as proxy nodes.
  • 03Lurking Lizard has impersonated major proxy providers including IPIDEA, SmartProxy, IP Royal, and 911Proxy, and has run fake independent review sites to drive traffic to its scam storefronts.
  • 04WHOIS analysis and infrastructure fingerprinting suggest that Lurking Lizard is a China-based actor, and the scheme has also used popular VPNs and services like HeroSMS as decoys to distribute proxy malware.
  • 05Google recently announced that it had significantly degraded the NetNut residential proxy network, which turned at least 2 million devices such as smart TVs and streaming boxes into conduits for unauthorized network traffic.

GodDamn Ransomware Uses PoisonX Driver to Disable Endpoint Defenses
thehackernews.com · 09 Jul 2026 10:43 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
TAGSanydeskbeastbroadcombyovdgentlekillergoddamnhyadinamicrosoftmonsternirsoftpoisonxpsexecqtoxsymantecthe-gentlemen

In plain words

Researchers found a new file-locking extortion program called GodDamn that attackers used in at least one organization in June 2026. The attackers used remote access software, stole saved passwords and other sensitive data, spread across multiple computers, and used a driver called PoisonX to turn off security tools before locking files. This matters because it shows the group behind GodDamn is improving its ability to break past defenses, putting targeted organizations at greater risk of disruption and data theft.

Summary
The new GodDamn ransomware, believed to be a rebrand of Beast/Monster, is using the Microsoft-signed PoisonX kernel driver in BYOVD attacks to disable endpoint security tools before encryption. Recent attacks also involved AnyDesk for remote access, NirSoft-based credential theft, PsExec lateral movement, and persistent AnyDesk deployment across hosts.

Cybersecurity researchers have identified a new ransomware family called GodDamn that uses the PoisonX kernel driver to disable security software as part of its defense evasion strategy. Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team said the ransomware was first publicly spotted in the wild on May 21, 2026. The company assesses GodDamn to be a rebrand of Beast ransomware, which was itself an enhanced version of Monster, and tracks the developer behind these families as Hyadina.

In an early June 2026 attack, the operators used AnyDesk for remote access and a NirSoft-based credential harvesting toolkit before deploying the ransomware. The toolkit was designed to extract sensitive data from browsers, Windows Credential Manager, cached domain credentials, VNC sessions, email clients, Wi-Fi profiles, and live network traffic. The attackers also used a user-mode defense evasion tool disguised as a Symantec product, named symantec.exe, together with the PoisonX driver, named g11.sys, in a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attack.

Symantec said PoisonX appears to be unusual because it looks like a malicious driver that its developers succeeded in getting signed by Microsoft. The attack also involved PsExec for lateral movement and repeated AnyDesk deployment across at least 10 hosts, with AnyDesk registered as an auto-start Windows service to survive reboots. GodDamn was later detected on June 3 on a separate network segment, and CYFIRMA reported that the ransom note instructed victims to contact the attackers by email or the qTox encrypted messaging app.

  • PoisonX is notable because Symantec says it appears to be a malicious driver that was nevertheless signed by Microsoft, making it different from typical bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attacks that rely on flawed but otherwise legitimate drivers.
  • GodDamn’s operators used a reusable-looking AnyDesk deployment process across at least 10 hosts, including installation as an auto-start Windows service, showing that remote access persistence was built into the intrusion before ransomware execution.
  • The same PoisonX driver has been adopted by The Gentlemen ransomware-as-a-service operation in its GentleKiller tool, indicating that this driver is being reused across more than one ransomware ecosystem.
  • In the observed attack, GodDamn used the victim’s name as the encrypted file extension rather than the .God8Damn extension seen in other Hyadina attacks, showing that file-renaming behavior may vary by victim or operation.
Key Points
  • 01Cybersecurity researchers identified a new ransomware family called GodDamn that uses the PoisonX kernel driver to disable security software as part of its defense evasion strategy.

Once inside, the group steals files from SharePoint, a Microsoft service many organizations use to store and share documents. This matters because the stolen information can be used to pressure companies into paying money or sold to other criminals.

Summary
A new extortion group called Helix is using vishing, device-code phishing, and MFA abuse to take over Microsoft 365 accounts and steal SharePoint data. Researchers say its tactics and infrastructure overlap with ShinyHunters and the defunct BlackFile group, and recommend disabling device-code authentication where possible.

A new data-extortion group called Helix is using identity-focused tactics to steal data from SharePoint environments. The group begins with voice phishing, sometimes calling employees while impersonating their manager through the manager’s name or caller ID spoofing. The goal is to trick targets into device-code phishing schemes that give the attackers access to their accounts.

Once inside, Helix operators quickly register a new multi-factor authenticator app for persistence, then browse and enumerate SharePoint before exfiltrating files. ReliaQuest researchers said the strongest technical fingerprint is automated SharePoint enumeration and collection from 179.43.185[.]230 using the python-requests/2.28.1 user-agent. The stolen data is typically used to extort victim organizations by threatening publication unless a ransom is paid, or it is sold to other cybercriminals.

ReliaQuest believes Helix may have emerged from the ShinyHunters and BlackFile data-extortion groups based on techniques and infrastructure, although it found no definitive connection. The researchers cited similarities including vishing, employee impersonation, Microsoft 365 targeting, SharePoint data theft, use of the NICENIC registrar, and an exfiltration IP in the same autonomous system as a confirmed BlackFile IP address. ReliaQuest recommends disabling device code authentication where possible, restricting SharePoint access to managed devices, and blocking exchanges with newly registered domains.

  • ReliaQuest identified Helix’s most reliable fingerprint as its SharePoint enumeration and bulk-download pattern, specifically activity from 179.43.185[.]230 using the python-requests/2.28.1 user-agent.

  • Helix appears to rely on persistence through registering a new multi-factor authenticator app immediately after gaining account access.
  • ReliaQuest noted that one Helix exfiltration IP address was in the same autonomous system, AS 51852, as a confirmed BlackFile IP address, suggesting possible shared resources.
  • Blocking exchanges with newly registered domains is specifically recommended because Helix typically uses such domains in its attacks.

In plain words

Microsoft released a fix for a problem in Microsoft Defender, the built-in protection software used on Windows, that could let someone gain the highest level of control on a computer. The issue could affect people and organizations using up-to-date Windows systems, even if Defender’s real-time protection was turned off. This matters because that level of control could let an attacker run programs or take actions they are not supposed to, but Microsoft says the update should be installed automatically for most users.

Summary
Microsoft patched the RoguePlanet flaw in its Malware Protection Engine, a Defender privilege-escalation vulnerability that could let attackers gain SYSTEM-level access on fully updated Windows systems. The fix is included in engine version 1.1.26060.3008 and should install automatically for most users.

Microsoft has released security updates for a Defender vulnerability known as RoguePlanet nearly a month after details of the flaw became public. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-50656 and has a CVSS score of 7.8. Microsoft said the issue has been remediated in Microsoft Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26060.3008, along with defense-in-depth updates to harden unspecified security-related features.

RoguePlanet is a privilege escalation issue in the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine, “mpengine.dll,” which provides scanning, detection, and cleaning capabilities for Microsoft antivirus and antispyware software. Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse described it as a race condition that could be abused to spawn a shell with SYSTEM-level privileges, allowing arbitrary code execution or unauthorized actions. The exploit was found to work on systems running up-to-date versions of Windows with the June 2026 Patch Tuesday updates installed, and the researcher said it worked regardless of whether real-time protection was enabled.

RoguePlanet is the fourth Defender vulnerability disclosed by Chaotic Eclipse after BlueHammer, UnDefend, and RedSun, all of which Microsoft has since patched. Microsoft said no customer action is required to install the update for CVE-2026-50656 because its antimalware software is frequently updated to protect customers against new and evolving threats. The company said enterprise and end-user default configurations help keep malware definitions and the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine updated automatically.

  • The exploit reportedly worked on fully updated Windows systems with the June 2026 Patch Tuesday updates installed, showing that normal monthly patching had not addressed this Defender issue before the engine update.
  • Chaotic Eclipse said the exploit worked whether Defender real-time protection was enabled or disabled, so turning off real-time protection was not described as a workaround.
  • Microsoft’s fix was delivered through the Malware Protection Engine update mechanism rather than requiring customer action, making engine version verification the clearest way to confirm remediation.
  • RoguePlanet was the fourth Defender vulnerability disclosed by the same researcher after BlueHammer, UnDefend, and RedSun, all of which Microsoft has since patched.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft released security updates for the Defender vulnerability known as RoguePlanet nearly a month after details of the flaw became public.
  • 02RoguePlanet is tracked as CVE-2026-50656 and is a privilege escalation issue in the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine, mpengine.dll.

In plain words

A fake software package called Braintree.Net was uploaded to NuGet to look like PayPal Braintree’s real payment library, but it secretly sent credit card details, merchant login keys, and other server secrets to an attacker-controlled website. The people most affected are developers and businesses that accidentally installed this fake package, especially if they used it in real payment systems. This matters because stolen card numbers, CVVs, and merchant keys can lead to fraud, exposure of customer payment data, and access to sensitive business systems.

Summary
A malicious NuGet typosquat, Braintree.Net, impersonated PayPal Braintree’s official SDK while stealing live payment card data, Braintree merchant API keys, and host secrets through a companion DependencyInjector.Core package. Any organization that used the affected packages should remove them, rotate credentials, investigate possible card-data exposure, and block the attacker domain.

Socket’s AI scanner flagged a suspicious NuGet package, Braintree.Net, masquerading as the official PayPal Braintree .NET SDK, with the first malicious version published on July 3, 2026. The package copied the surface API, README content, metadata, and project URL of the legitimate Braintree library while using a different package name and version scheme. Socket’s Threat Research team found that affected versions routed stolen data to attacker-controlled infrastructure at api.348672-shakepay[.]com.

The malicious package intercepted live payment card data and stole Braintree merchant API credentials when used in production. Its added CardOperationLogger hooked payment-related methods to send card numbers, CVVs, expiration dates, customer IDs, amounts, and related transaction details to /api/card. Its modified BraintreeGateway.PrivateKey setter sent the merchantId, publicKey, and privateKey to /api/account when the gateway was configured for Braintree’s production environment.

Starting with Braintree.Net 3.36.0, the package also depended on DependencyInjector.Core, which used module initializers to run on assembly load and harvest environment variables, configuration files, cloud and container metadata, dependencies, and loaded assemblies. The article also identifies related affected packages, including DependencyInjector.Core, SipNet, and SipNet.OpenAI.Realtime, and notes that some were affected transitively. Recommended actions include removing Braintree.Net, replacing it with the official Braintree package, rotating Braintree credentials, treating production card data as potentially disclosed, auditing dependency graphs, blocking the attacker domain, and hunting for outbound POSTs to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.

  • The package’s reported popularity was misleading: roughly 11 million of its approximately 14 million downloads came from 120 empty placeholder versions, while the confirmed malicious releases had only about 334 real installs.
  • The payment-card and merchant-credential theft paths activated only for Braintree production environments, which reduced the chance of discovery during sandbox or development testing.
  • The companion DependencyInjector.Core harvester ran on assembly load through module initializers, so victim applications could leak environment and configuration secrets without calling any malicious API directly.
  • The attacker used different hiding strategies for different payloads: the card and account theft endpoints were plaintext strings, while the broader analytics/report endpoint was XOR-obfuscated.
  • SipNet became malicious through a manifest-only dependency change for .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10 targets, while its own DLL remained a clean recompile of SIPSorcery.
Key Points
  • 01Socket’s AI scanner flagged a malicious NuGet package named Braintree.Net that masqueraded as PayPal Braintree’s official .NET SDK and routed stolen data to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.
  • 02Confirmed malicious Braintree.Net versions 3.35.8 through 3.36.1 intercepted live payment card data, including full card numbers, CVVs, expiration dates, customer IDs, amounts, operations, gateways, card types, and timestamps.
  • 03The typosquat stole Braintree merchant credentials by sending merchantId, publicKey, and privateKey values to the attacker endpoint when a production gateway was configured.
  • 04Starting with Braintree.Net 3.36.0, the package depended on DependencyInjector.Core, which used module initializers to collect environment variables, appsettings JSON contents, cloud and container metadata, dependencies, and loaded assemblies on assembly load.
  • 05Socket recommended removing Braintree.Net, replacing it with the official Braintree package, rotating Braintree merchant credentials, auditing for DependencyInjector.Core, SipNet, and SipNet.OpenAI.Realtime, and hunting for outbound POSTs to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.

In plain words

Microsoft found a harmful Windows program called GigaWiper, also reported as BLUERABBIT, that lets attackers secretly watch a computer and then destroy it in several ways, including wiping the disk or scrambling files with no way to unlock them. Reports link the same files and servers to activity aimed at Israeli organizations, with some evidence pointing to a likely Iran-linked group, though Microsoft did not name a country. This matters because once attackers are already inside a computer, this tool can turn spying into total data loss, so affected organizations may only recover by rebuilding machines from clean backups.

Summary
Microsoft analyzed GigaWiper, a Windows backdoor also tracked as BLUERABBIT, that combines spying capabilities with multiple destructive options including disk wiping and fake ransomware that cannot be decrypted. Defenders should treat it as a post-compromise tool and prioritize early detection, blocking known command servers, and maintaining clean offline backups.

Microsoft analyzed a destructive Windows backdoor it calls GigaWiper, which combines three older destructive programs into operator-selectable commands. The same malicious files are also tracked by Binary Defense as BLUERABBIT, with both vendors listing the same four hashes and matching command servers. Binary Defense, citing Google’s Threat Intelligence Group, ties the malware to a likely Iran-nexus group aimed at Israeli organizations, while Microsoft does not name a country.

GigaWiper can wipe a physical drive and its partition table, run fake ransomware based on Crucio that encrypts files with no saved key, or overwrite the Windows drive using a Go rewrite of FlockWiper. The article emphasizes that these functions are destructive rather than financially motivated, because wiped drives and files encrypted without a retained key cannot be restored except from clean backups. The backdoor also has spying and control features, including screenshots, screen recording, hidden VNC access, system information collection, registry editing, and event log wiping.

To hide, GigaWiper pretends to be OneDrive by creating a scheduled task named OneDrive Update that runs every minute and tracking itself under a OneDrive-related registry key. It uses RabbitMQ for tasking, Redis for results, and MinIO for exfiltration, which may look ordinary on networks that already run those legitimate services. Microsoft recommends watching for the recurring OneDrive Update task, RabbitMQ or Redis traffic from ordinary desktops, suspicious use of takeown and icacls against Windows boot files, and blocking the known command servers 185.182.193[.]21 and 212.8.248[.]104.

  • GigaWiper’s fake ransomware behavior can mislead responders because the .candy file encryption and warning wallpaper resemble ransomware, but the article says no key is saved and no ransom path exists, making recovery dependent on clean backups rather than negotiation or decryption.
  • The backdoor’s use of RabbitMQ, Redis, and MinIO for command traffic, results, and data theft is especially actionable because the article notes this traffic may look ordinary on networks that already run those legitimate business services.
  • A single GigaWiper infection does not reveal the attacker’s final intent because the same implant can spy, steal, or destroy depending on which commands the operator chooses after gaining access.
  • The overlap between Microsoft’s GigaWiper reporting and Binary Defense’s BLUERABBIT reporting shows that two vendor names refer to the same set of files and command servers, which can help defenders unify detections and intelligence.
  • The dormant keylogger and additional wiper command stubs found by Microsoft indicate the tool was not limited to its observed capabilities and may have been designed for further expansion.

  • 04The backdoor can take screenshots, record the screen, open a hidden VNC session, collect system details, manage programs and services, edit the registry, and wipe Windows event logs.

In plain words

Researchers at Wiz found that several popular AI coding assistants can be tricked by a malicious code project into changing important files on a developer’s computer while showing approval prompts that name a harmless-looking file instead. The affected tools include Amazon Q Developer, Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf, with some fixed and others still not fully fixed. This matters because the trick could let an attacker add their own login key or make code run the next time a developer opens a terminal, showing that “human approval” is not enough if the person is shown the wrong information.

Summary
Wiz researchers found “GhostApproval,” a symlink flaw in several AI coding assistants that can make a malicious repository trick agents into writing to sensitive files like SSH keys or shell startup scripts while showing users a misleading approval prompt. Some vendors have patched, but users should update tools and avoid running agents on untrusted repositories without sandboxing or limited file access.

Researchers at Wiz found a flaw in six popular AI coding assistants that could let a malicious code project quietly take control of a developer’s computer. The affected tools are Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic’s Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf. Wiz calls the pattern GhostApproval and says it allows an assistant to ask permission to edit a harmless-looking file while the actual write lands on a sensitive file instead.

The attack abuses symbolic links, which are files that point to other files elsewhere on disk. In Wiz’s example, a malicious repository used a file named project_settings.json that actually pointed to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, so an instruction to add a line to the project file could add an attacker’s SSH key to the victim’s login file. Another version writes to ~/.zshrc, which can run commands the next time a terminal is opened, and Wiz said there is no sign the technique has been used in real attacks.

Wiz reported the issue to all six vendors, and Amazon Q Developer, Cursor, and Google Antigravity have shipped fixes. Augment and Windsurf acknowledged the issue but had no fix at publication, while Anthropic disputed that Claude Code’s behavior is a bug and said current versions warn users about symlinks. Wiz recommends that tool makers resolve symlinks and show the real destination before approval, flag writes outside the project folder, and avoid touching disk until the user has actually approved.

  • The highest-risk tools are not necessarily the ones with no approval prompt; Windsurf showed Accept and Reject buttons only after writing the file to disk, making the prompt function as an undo mechanism rather than a true approval gate.
  • Wiz observed that Claude Code’s internal reasoning could identify the real symlink target while the developer-facing approval box still displayed only the harmless-looking path, showing a gap between what the agent knows and what it tells the user.
  • The issue affects files outside the project directory, so a developer may not see evidence of the change in git status and must check files such as shell startup files, SSH keys, and AI tool configuration separately.
  • Two independent research efforts, Wiz’s GhostApproval and Adversa AI’s SymJack, found the same symlink-and-approval pattern across multiple coding agents, indicating a shared design weakness rather than an isolated vendor mistake.
Key Points
  • 01Wiz researchers found a flaw they call GhostApproval in six AI coding assistants: Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf.
  • 02The attack uses a symlink in a malicious repository so that an assistant asked to edit a harmless-looking file actually writes to a sensitive file such as ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or ~/.zshrc.
  • 03Wiz says the approval prompt can show the harmless file name instead of the real destination, creating an informed-consent bypass where the user approves an edit without seeing where it will actually land.
  • 04Amazon Q Developer, Cursor, and Google Antigravity have shipped fixes, Augment and Windsurf have acknowledged the issue without fixes yet, and Anthropic disputes that the Claude Code behavior is a bug.
  • 05Wiz recommends that tool makers resolve symlinks and show the real destination before approval, flag writes outside the project folder, and avoid writing to disk until the user has approved.

    In plain words

    The article is a roundup of recent security stories, including global fraud arrests, fake software packages, fake IT support calls, ransomware, phishing, and cloud storage tricks that can quietly send a company’s data to an attacker. People, businesses, developers, government groups, and cloud users are affected because many of these problems start from normal-looking tools, messages, settings, or account names. The broader risk is that small everyday gaps can lead to stolen money, stolen accounts, exposed private data, and attackers gaining control before anyone notices.

    Summary
    This week’s threats show how ordinary operational gaps—reused cloud bucket names, trusted remote tools, typosquatted packages, stale credentials, and loose egress controls—can quickly become paths for data theft, privilege escalation, and ransomware. The key takeaway is to scrutinize normal-looking workflows and permissions before attackers turn them into quiet compromise channels.

    This ThreatsDay roundup covers 20 security stories centered on ordinary administrative gaps becoming serious risks. It includes a global fraud operation that led to 5,811 arrests and the interception of $293 million, malicious npm and PyPI packages typosquatting payment SDKs, and a critical Esri ArcGIS Server flaw that could allow unauthenticated access to sensitive files. The article also highlights social engineering campaigns using Microsoft Teams, Meta Business Account Manager, tax refund lures, and remote access tools to steal credentials or deploy malware.

    Several items focus on technical methods that avoid detection or abuse trusted systems. Researchers described Process Parameter Poisoning for stealthy code injection, a Windows local privilege escalation chain involving RPC spoofing and the Data Sharing Service, and multiple flaws in Realtek’s RtsPer.sys driver that could expose kernel memory or allow physical memory access. Other reports covered GhostChrome-X modifying Chrome extension integrity metadata, fileless and steganographic Remcos delivery, and ransomware activity involving Interlock, Rhysida, WhiteLock, Prinz Eugen, Bumblebee, AdaptixC2, and Akira.

    Cloud and identity risks are a major theme across the roundup. Mandiant warned that manually rotated ADFS certificates can leave active signing keys exposed through Machine DPAPI, creating a risk of forged high-privilege SAML tokens, while AWS emphasized layered egress controls to reduce data exfiltration risk. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 described cloud bucket hijacking, where deleting and recreating a globally unique bucket name under another account can reroute logs and sensitive data to an attacker-controlled environment.

    • Several campaigns relied on legitimate or trusted channels, including Microsoft Teams, Meta Business Account Manager, Chrome extensions, remote management tools, and cloud storage services, showing that normal business tools can become attacker infrastructure when permissions and trust are too broad.
    • The cloud bucket hijacking risk is especially actionable because it depends on globally unique bucket names: deleting and recreating a bucket name under another account can silently redirect active data streams without exploiting a software bug.
    • Multiple items show attackers designing malware to avoid early detection, including packages that skip sandbox-like machines, fileless Remcos execution, Process Parameter Poisoning, and GhostChrome-X forging Chrome extension integrity metadata.
    • Old or leftover trusted state created major exposure in more than one case, including manually rotated ADFS signing keys remaining recoverable through Machine DPAPI and reused cloud bucket names becoming hijackable after deletion.
    • Remote access tools were both targeted and abused: WhiteLock terminates AnyDesk and TeamViewer to block defenders, while fake Teams support campaigns guided victims into installing HopToDesk and AnyDesk for attacker persistence.

In plain words

Police agencies working together through INTERPOL arrested 5,811 people in 97 countries and seized $293 million linked to scams and moving stolen money. The operation focused on crimes like fake business emails, sextortion, impersonation, romance scams, and investment scams, and investigators identified more than 142,000 victims worldwide. This matters because these scams affect individuals, businesses, and governments across borders, and the article shows that stopping them requires countries to work together.

Summary
INTERPOL-coordinated Operation First Light 2026 led to 5,811 arrests across 97 countries and the seizure of $293 million tied to social engineering fraud and money laundering. Authorities identified over 142,000 victims and blocked more than 31,000 bank accounts, underscoring the global scale of cyber-enabled financial scams.

Law enforcement agencies arrested 5,811 suspects and seized $293 million in illicit assets during a global anti-fraud operation spanning 97 countries. The joint action, dubbed Operation First Light 2026, targeted social engineering fraud and money laundering activities between January 15 and April 30. The fraud types included business email compromise, sextortion, impersonation, romance scams, and investment scams.

INTERPOL said the operation included action against high-value targets, raids on identified premises, blocking or freezing bank accounts and virtual wallets, and requests for INTERPOL Notices and Diffusions. Authorities also used INTERPOL’s Global Rapid Intervention of Payments, a stop-payment mechanism designed to swiftly block illicit financial flows involving both fiat and virtual assets. Investigators identified more than 142,000 victims worldwide, blocked 31,014 bank accounts, analyzed 152,808 cases, and identified 15,606 suspects beyond those arrested.

Operation First Light 2026 was coordinated by INTERPOL, funded by China’s Ministry of Public Security, and supported by ASEANAPOL, GCCPOL, and Europol. INTERPOL said the number of victims shows that social engineering scams and fraud have escalated into a major transnational threat affecting individuals, businesses, and governments. Tomonobu Kaya of the INTERPOL Financial Crime and Anti-Corruption Centre said criminal syndicates exploit human psychology and that countries must be equipped and committed to jointly fighting back.

  • The operation treated fraud and money laundering as one connected problem, using both arrests and financial disruption measures such as freezing bank accounts, virtual wallets, and illicit payment flows.
  • INTERPOL’s I-GRIP mechanism was used to block illicit movement of both traditional money and virtual assets, showing that rapid payment intervention is now part of international anti-fraud operations.
  • The number of additional identified suspects, 15,606, was far higher than the 5,811 arrests, indicating that the operation produced a large pipeline of unresolved investigative targets.
  • The operation’s scope across 97 countries and more than 142,000 identified victims supports INTERPOL’s statement that social engineering scams have become a major transnational threat affecting individuals, businesses, and governments.
Key Points
  • 01Law enforcement agencies arrested 5,811 suspects and seized $293 million in illicit assets during Operation First Light 2026, a global anti-fraud operation spanning 97 countries.
  • 02Operation First Light 2026 targeted social engineering fraud, including business email compromise, sextortion, impersonation, romance, and investment scams, as well as money laundering activities between January 15 and April 30.
  • 03Investigators identified more than 142,000 victims worldwide, blocked 31,014 bank accounts, analyzed 152,808 cases, and identified 15,606 additional suspects beyond those arrested.
  • 04The operation was coordinated by INTERPOL, funded by China’s Ministry of Public Security, and supported by ASEANAPOL, GCCPOL, and Europol.
  • 05INTERPOL said the operation included action against high-value targets, raids on identified premises, blocking or freezing bank accounts and virtual wallets, and use of its Global Rapid Intervention of Payments stop-payment mechanism.

In plain words

A new service called Forg365 helps criminals create convincing fake Microsoft 365 sign-in messages and pages, including messages generated with AI. It is aimed at stealing access to Microsoft 365 accounts, which can affect people and organizations that use Microsoft’s email and work services. This matters because the service can help attackers stay logged in to stolen accounts and search victims’ mailboxes for useful information.

Summary
Forg365 is a new phishing-as-a-service platform targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with device-code and AiTM phishing, AI-generated lures, and a browser extension that refreshes stolen session cookies for persistent access. Defenders should restrict device-code authentication and monitor Entra, OAuth grants, mailbox rules, and session activity for signs of compromise.

A new phishing-as-a-service operation called Forg365 targets Microsoft 365 accounts by combining adversary-in-the-middle and device-code phishing methods with AI-assisted lure generation. ZeroBEC researchers say the platform includes features seen in other phishing services such as Kali365 and Sneaky2FA, though they could not establish a connection. Their investigation began with phishing emails posing as business documents and using legitimate services such as Amazon SES and SendGrid-hosted resources.

ZeroBEC obtained access to the Forg365 dashboard, which can create phishing campaigns, manage links, configure OAuth apps and SMTP profiles, manage tokens, and generate phishing emails with AI. The researchers highlighted that AI lure generation is directly integrated into the same panel used to control post-compromise activity. The panel also includes account intelligence features and keyword monitoring that scans compromised mailboxes for predefined terms.

Forg365 provides a browser extension called ForgCookie for Chrome, Edge, and Brave that is designed to refresh Microsoft single sign-on cookies and maintain access to services tied to compromised accounts. The platform supports device-code phishing, where victims are tricked into authorizing an attacker-controlled device through Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth 2.0 device code flow, and AiTM phishing, where a proxy captures session cookies. ZeroBEC recommends restricting or disabling Microsoft device-code authentication unless needed, monitoring Microsoft Entra logs, investigating unexpected mailbox rules and OAuth grants, and revoking tokens and sessions if compromise is suspected.

  • Forg365’s AI email-writing feature is embedded in the same dashboard used for token management and post-compromise activity, making lure creation part of a single end-to-end phishing workflow rather than a separate step.
  • The platform’s ForgCookie extension is designed to refresh Microsoft single sign-on cookies automatically, showing that Forg365 focuses not only on initial account theft but also on maintaining continued access after compromise.
  • Forg365 blends phishing activity with legitimate services such as Amazon SES, SendGrid, Cloudflare Pages, and Gophish, which can make malicious traffic resemble ordinary business email and web activity.
  • The device-code phishing path does not require directly stealing a victim’s password; it tricks the victim into approving an attacker-controlled device through Microsoft’s legitimate device-code sign-in flow.
  • Forg365 includes defensive evasion features such as encrypted redirectors, bot detection, debugger traps, sandbox checks, polymorphic code, and VPN-based redirection to keep researchers away from its phishing pages and administration panel.
Key Points
  • 01Forg365 is a phishing-as-a-service operation focused on stealing Microsoft 365 accounts using adversary-in-the-middle phishing, device-code phishing, and AI-assisted lure generation.
  • 02ZeroBEC researchers gained access to the Forg365 dashboard, which can create phishing campaigns, manage phishing links, configure OAuth apps and SMTP profiles, manage tokens, and generate phishing emails with AI.
  • 03Forg365 includes a browser extension called ForgCookie that refreshes Microsoft single sign-on cookies to help attackers maintain access to Microsoft services linked to compromised accounts.
  • 04The platform uses legitimate services and infrastructure including Amazon SES for phishing email delivery, SendGrid-hosted resources, Cloudflare Pages for landing pages, and Gophish for campaign delivery.
  • 05ZeroBEC recommends restricting or disabling Microsoft device-code authentication unless required, monitoring Microsoft Entra logs, investigating unexpected mailbox rules and OAuth grants, and revoking tokens and sessions if compromise is suspected.

It is not a breach or critical patch, but it provides actionable detection and mitigation guidance for a widely used enterprise platform.

In plain words

Researchers at the AI Now Institute showed that AI coding tools from Anthropic and OpenAI can be fooled into running harmful code when they are set to work on their own while checking outside software. This affects people and teams who use Claude Code or OpenAI Codex to inspect code they did not create, especially if those tools can run commands on the same computer that holds their files, passwords, or keys. It matters because these tools are being promoted for finding security problems, but in this setup they can become the way an attacker gets in instead.

Summary
AI Now researchers showed that Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can be tricked into running malicious code while autonomously reviewing untrusted repositories, using benign-looking README instructions and disguised binaries. The key takeaway is that security teams should not let command-capable AI coding agents inspect third-party code with access to the host, secrets, or keys unless strong isolation and human approval are in place.

AI Now Institute published a proof-of-concept called “Friendly Fire” showing that AI coding agents can be tricked into running attacker-controlled code while reviewing untrusted open-source projects. The attack worked against Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex when their autonomous modes were enabled, allowing the tools to approve commands they judged safe. The researchers argue there is no specific patch or vulnerable version range because the issue is a workflow design problem rather than a single software bug.

The demo used the Python library geopy with added files, including a README.md note that suggested running a script called security.sh as a routine security check. When given a prompt such as “Perform security testing on this project,” the agent read the README, treated the script as part of the task, and ran it without a warning or approval box. The script quietly launched a hidden binary disguised as the compiled build of a harmless Go file, and the researchers seeded it with strings from that file to help it pass the agent’s checks.

The article says this route is broader than earlier attacks that abused agent configuration files, because README.md is an ordinary file in nearly every repository and does not trigger Claude Code’s folder trust warning. The same payload worked unchanged across Claude Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.5, and in some runs newer models noticed the binary mismatch but still executed it. The researchers recommend not giving untrusted code to an agent that can run commands and access keys, secrets, or the host, while noting that sandboxing and step-by-step approvals are only partial mitigations.

  • The attack avoids prior defenses focused on agent configuration files by hiding instructions in a README.md file, which is common in repositories and does not trigger Claude Code’s folder trust warning.
  • The same payload worked unchanged across two vendors and four models, and in some runs newer models noticed the binary mismatch but executed it anyway.
  • AI Now says there is no specific patch or vulnerable version range to wait for, because the tested builds were examples and the researchers view the issue as a workflow design problem.
  • A practical warning sign is an agent executing a binary or script that is only recommended by documentation rather than invoked by the project’s own code.
  • Sandboxing may reduce risk but is not presented as a reliable fix, because the article notes that code can escape sandboxes and cites a Claude Code sandbox escape flaw from this year.
Key Points
  • 01AI Now Institute researchers published a proof-of-concept called Friendly Fire that tricks Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex into running attacker-controlled code while reviewing untrusted open-source projects in autonomous modes.
  • 02The researchers tested stock installs of Claude Code CLI versions 2.1.116, 2.1.196, 2.1.198, and 2.1.199 with Claude Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, or Opus 4.8, and OpenAI Codex CLI 0.142.4 with GPT-5.5.
  • 03The demo placed extra files in the geopy Python library, including README instructions to run security.sh, which quietly launched a hidden binary disguised as the compiled build of a harmless Go file.
  • 04AI Now argues the weakness is in the design rather than a specific vulnerable version, because the models cannot reliably separate code and documentation they are reading from instructions they should follow.
  • 05The researchers recommend not giving untrusted code to an agent that can run commands and access keys, secrets, or the host, and note that sandboxing and approval prompts are only partial mitigations in the tested scenario.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a specific, recent proof-of-concept affecting widely used AI coding agents in a security-review workflow, with broad relevance for teams using autonomous code-review tools on untrusted repositories. It is not active exploitation in the wild and has no immediate patch, but the finding is actionable because it changes how such tools should be used around host access, secrets, and command execution.

In plain words

Datadog Security Labs says attackers are using old, inactive GitHub accounts and stolen access keys from real users to quietly look through companies’ GitHub pages and accounts. They mostly collected public information about company projects and the people connected to them, but in a few cases they also copied private code from a company. This matters because the activity can help attackers map how an organization works and, in the worst cases, reach sensitive software that was not meant to be public.

Summary
Datadog Security Labs warns that attackers are using years-old dormant GitHub “ghost” accounts and compromised tokens to quietly enumerate corporate GitHub orgs, repos, and users via the GitHub API. Most activity targets public data for reconnaissance, but some cases escalated to cloning private repositories.

Datadog Security Labs warned of several overlapping campaigns systematically enumerating corporate GitHub organizations, repositories, and user accounts through the GitHub API. The operators rely on automated scraping tools with custom or legitimate-sounding user agents. They also use GitHub “ghost” accounts that are often years old, along with compromised OAuth tokens and personal access tokens from legitimate users.

Most of the activity targets public data, but Datadog said some cases went beyond public information enumeration. In a few scenarios, data access was confirmed and attackers took steps to clone a private repository belonging to a single organization. The campaign used more than 50 dormant accounts and dozens of legitimate accounts whose personal access tokens were exposed unintentionally or compromised through some other method.

The “ghost” accounts were created two to five years ago and intentionally left inactive for long periods before being used to issue API traffic across multiple organizations. Datadog said this helps the activity blend into normal GitHub API usage, especially because many API requests hit public endpoints and return successful responses. The concern is the aggregate pattern of accounts moving in sync across companies’ GitHub organizations over weeks, and in the worst case shifting from enumeration to cloning.

  • The use of GitHub accounts created two to five years earlier shows the operators deliberately built or preserved credibility over long periods before using the accounts for scraping.
  • The activity is difficult to spot because individual requests often look normal, hit public endpoints, and may not require authentication at all.
  • The main warning sign is not a single suspicious request but coordinated behavior across multiple accounts and companies over weeks.
  • Reconnaissance against public GitHub data can still create real risk because it can map an organization’s repositories, members, relationships, and project activity.
  • The same campaigns that mostly enumerate public data have, in some confirmed cases, progressed to cloning private repositories.
Key Points
  • 01Datadog Security Labs warned of several overlapping campaigns systematically enumerating corporate GitHub organizations, repositories, and user accounts through the GitHub API.
  • 02The operators use automated scraping tools with custom or legitimate-sounding user agents, GitHub “ghost” accounts that are often years old, and compromised OAuth tokens or personal access tokens from legitimate users.
  • 03More than 50 dormant accounts and dozens of legitimate accounts with exposed or compromised personal access tokens were used to facilitate the enumeration.
  • 04The GitHub “ghost” accounts were created two to five years ago and left inactive for long periods before being used to issue API traffic across multiple organizations.
  • 05Most activity involved public data, but Datadog confirmed a few scenarios where attackers went beyond enumeration and cloned a private repository belonging to a single organization.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a specific finding about active, coordinated GitHub API enumeration campaigns affecting corporate GitHub organizations, with some confirmed cases escalating to private repository cloning. It is broadly relevant to security professionals because the activity blends into normal API usage and uses dormant accounts plus compromised tokens, making detection more difficult.

npm 12 Disables Install Scripts by Default to Reduce Supply Chain Risk

In plain words

GitHub has released npm 12, changing how JavaScript software packages are installed so that extra commands from packages and downloads from certain outside sources no longer run automatically unless developers approve them. This affects developers and organizations that use npm, especially those with automated publishing or security settings that previously relied on special tokens to skip two-factor checks. The goal is to reduce the chance that a malicious or compromised package can quietly run harmful code or misuse publishing access, which matters because npm is widely used to build software many people depend on.

Summary
GitHub released npm 12 with install scripts, Git dependencies, and remote URL dependencies disabled by default to reduce supply chain risk. It is also phasing out 2FA-bypass granular access tokens for sensitive npm actions and direct publishing, pushing maintainers toward trusted publishing or human approval workflows.

GitHub announced the release of npm version 12 with install scripts disabled by default. The release also deprecates granular access tokens designed to bypass two-factor authentication. GitHub said several npm install behaviors that previously ran automatically are now opt-in.

In npm 12, dependency lifecycle scripts such as preinstall, install, and postinstall no longer run unless explicitly allowed. Implicit node-gyp builds are also disabled by default, and Git dependencies or dependencies from remote URLs are no longer resolved unless explicitly allowed. To review and approve trusted scripts, users must run “npm approve-scripts –allow-scripts-pending” and commit the resulting allowlist in package.json.

GitHub also said npm granular access tokens configured to bypass two-factor authentication will lose access to sensitive account, package, and organization management actions in early August 2026. In January 2027, those tokens will no longer be able to publish directly, and GitHub recommends moving automated publishing to trusted publishing using OIDC or staged publishing with human approval. The article also notes that pnpm 11.10 introduced a new “_auth” setting intended to keep registry credentials tied to the host they belong to and prevent project files from redirecting valid tokens.

  • npm 12 makes previously automatic install-time behaviors opt-in, so projects may need to commit an explicit script allowlist in package.json to preserve trusted build steps.
  • GitHub is creating a transition window for token changes: sensitive management actions using 2FA-bypass tokens are affected in early August 2026, while direct publishing with those tokens remains available until January 2027.
  • The article points maintainers away from long-lived publish tokens and toward trusted publishing using OIDC or staged publishing with a human approval step.
  • pnpm 11.10’s new _auth handling reduces token exposure by reading authentication only from the environment or global config, not from project files that could be tampered with.
Key Points
  • 01GitHub announced the release of npm version 12 with install scripts disabled by default and deprecated granular access tokens designed to bypass two-factor authentication.
  • 02In npm 12, dependency lifecycle scripts and implicit node-gyp builds no longer run unless explicitly allowed, and Git dependencies or remote URL dependencies are no longer resolved unless explicitly allowed.
  • 03Users must run “npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending” to review and approve trusted scripts, then commit the resulting allowlist in the package.json file.
  • 04In early August 2026, npm granular access tokens configured to bypass two-factor authentication will no longer be able to perform sensitive account, package, and organization management actions.
  • 05In January 2027, npm granular access tokens will no longer be able to publish directly, and GitHub recommends moving automated publishing to trusted publishing using OIDC or staged publishing with human approval.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a specific npm release announcement with broad relevance to software supply chain security, because npm 12 changes default install behavior and restricts 2FA-bypass tokens. It is not an active exploitation report or emergency patch, but it affects many developers and organizations that rely on npm workflows.
