Summary
Microsoft says Windows users should expect more security fixes in monthly Patch Tuesday updates as AI tools help the company find and validate more vulnerabilities faster. The company says human engineers will still review fixes before release, while it updates its secure development practices for AI-enabled threats.

Microsoft says Windows users should expect an increase in security updates as the company uses artificial intelligence to find more vulnerabilities in its codebase. In a blog post, Microsoft said AI advances are accelerating vulnerability discovery, helping engineers identify more issues before they can be exploited in zero-day attacks. The company said customers will likely see a higher volume of security updates in each monthly Patch Tuesday release.

Microsoft is using Microsoft Security’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, MDASH, to scan critical Windows binaries and validate potential vulnerabilities with multiple AI models. Vulnerability candidates then go through a Windows-specific validation pipeline designed to eliminate false positives before engineers investigate them. Microsoft said it is also using AI to help engineers understand failures faster, suggest possible fixes, and find similar bugs elsewhere in the Windows source code.

Microsoft said human engineers will still oversee and review all proposed code and validate fixes before release into production. The company is also updating its Secure Development Lifecycle practices to account for AI-enabled attack techniques and to use AI earlier in software development. The article also notes a Reuters report that CISA has begun using Anthropic’s Fable AI model to scan government software for vulnerabilities.

  • Microsoft’s use of multiple AI models plus a separate Windows-specific validation pipeline shows that AI-generated vulnerability findings still require filtering before engineers treat them as actionable.
  • Microsoft is applying AI beyond initial bug discovery by using it to understand failures, suggest fixes, and search for similar bugs elsewhere in the Windows source code.
  • The article frames AI as affecting both sides of security: Microsoft is using it to find and fix flaws faster, while threat actors are using it to power attacks and exploit zero-day flaws before fixes exist.

Summary
Latvia’s state-owned forestry company LVM is still restoring systems weeks after a ransomware attack that disrupted services and exposed 44 GB of stolen data. Authorities say the same financially motivated foreign group is still probing Latvian public- and private-sector targets, but election infrastructure was not compromised.

Latvia’s state-owned forestry company LVM said it is still restoring IT systems weeks after a ransomware attack disrupted several internal and customer services. The attack took its mapping platform, hunting application, and systems used to exchange information with contractors and customers offline. LVM’s chief technology officer said the situation has stabilized, but returning operations to normal remains quite challenging. About two-thirds of customers with service contracts still do not have access to the affected systems.

According to LVM’s chief technology officer, the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a system that had not been updated for two years, though the affected software was not identified. Latvian authorities said the attackers had likely been inside the company’s network for more than a week before detection. CERT.LV attributed the intrusion to a foreign, financially motivated ransomware group that has previously targeted companies and public institutions in NATO and European Union countries. The attackers leaked roughly 44 gigabytes of stolen data, including internal documents, email correspondence, software code repositories, digital certificates, cryptographic keys, and user credentials.

The incident drew scrutiny because LVM helped develop new functionality for Latvia’s electronic voter registration system, but authorities said the election infrastructure was not compromised. CERT.LV said the election software was developed in a separate environment, its code was never stored in LVM’s corporate repositories, and every software delivery for the project was reviewed. CERT.LV also said the same threat actor compromised a server belonging to Latvian pharmaceutical company Olpha, though that breach has been contained and was technically unrelated to the LVM incident.

  • A single unpatched system that had not been updated for two years was enough to create a prolonged operational disruption for LVM, with about two-thirds of service-contract customers still lacking access weeks later.

  • CERT.LV specifically validated the election-related software delivery chain after the LVM breach, showing that separation of development environments and code repositories was central to ruling out compromise of the voter registration system.

In plain words

The European Commission is taking Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the EU’s top court because they have not put a major EU cyber safety law into their national rules. The law is meant to set basic protections and reporting duties for services people rely on every day, including hospitals, energy networks, transport operators and public offices. This matters because the EU’s cyber agency has warned of thousands of incidents across the bloc, and officials say power grids, hospitals and financial systems are increasingly exposed to disruption.

Summary
The European Commission is taking Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the EU’s top court for failing to implement the NIS2 cybersecurity directive, seeking financial penalties until they comply. The law sets minimum security and reporting requirements for critical sectors such as hospitals, energy, transport and public administration.

The European Commission filed legal referrals at the Court of Justice of the European Union against Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands for failing to implement the NIS2 Directive. The countries are more than 20 months late in transposing the law, which sets minimum security standards for hospitals, energy networks, transport operators and public administrations. The Commission asked the court to impose a lump sum and ongoing daily financial penalties until each country formally notifies full transposition.

NIS2 updates the original 2016 Network and Information Security Directive by widening its scope to 18 critical sectors and adding risk management and incident reporting requirements. Few member states met the original October 2024 deadline, and as of January 2025 only six of the EU’s 27 member states had transposed the directive. In practice, fines sought by the Commission are rarely paid because member states have generally adopted the required legislation while proceedings are under way, leading the Commission to withdraw before a court ruling.

The filing comes as ENISA warned of thousands of cybersecurity incidents affecting the EU in the year ending June 2025, with public administration the most-targeted critical sector at 38% of incidents and transport at 7.5%. Commission technology lead Henna Virkkunen warned in February that the EU could no longer afford to be “naive” about adversaries’ ability to switch off critical infrastructure, including power grids, hospitals and financial systems. Ireland said its National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose NIS2 and place the National Cyber Security Centre on a statutory footing, is close to finalization, while Spain, France and the Netherlands had not published comparable statements at the time of writing.

  • The Commission’s requested fines may function more as pressure to accelerate national legislation than as penalties that are ultimately paid, because previous member-state cases were often withdrawn once required laws were adopted during proceedings.
  • NIS2 delays have knock-on effects beyond the directive itself, because the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act relies on the national response-team network that NIS2 is supposed to establish.
  • The implementation gap is bloc-wide rather than limited to the four countries taken to court, since only six of the EU’s 27 member states had transposed NIS2 by January 2025.
  • The enforcement action comes as EU officials are simultaneously proposing amendments to NIS2 to ease compliance, indicating that legal clarity and company compliance burdens have been recognized as contributors to transposition delays.
Key Points
  • 01The European Commission filed legal referrals at the Court of Justice of the European Union against Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands for failing to implement the NIS2 Directive.
  • 02The NIS2 Directive sets minimum security standards for critical sectors including hospitals, energy networks, transport operators and public administrations.
  • 03The Commission asked the court to impose lump sum and ongoing daily financial penalties on the four countries until each formally notifies full transposition.
  • 04ENISA warned of thousands of cybersecurity incidents affecting the EU in the year ending June 2025, with public administration identified as the most-targeted critical sector at 38% of incidents.
  • 05Ireland said its National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose NIS2 and place the National Cyber Security Centre on a statutory footing, is close to finalization.

In plain words

A logistics company received an email that looked like an official transportation compliance notice because it used real government wording and the company’s actual USDOT number, then pushed the company to pay for an update that can be done for free on the official FMCSA site. Trucking carriers and their staff are affected because a real public identifier and a real deadline can make a paid solicitation feel like a government demand. Summary
A logistics carrier received a convincing FMCSA-themed payment solicitation that used its real USDOT number and legitimate compliance language to sell a free MCS-150 update. The key warning is to verify regulatory notices directly through official government portals, not links in emails, because public identifiers and accurate terminology do not prove legitimacy.

A logistics carrier received an email titled “Required FMCSA Biennial Update” that included the carrier’s genuine USDOT number and warned about fines and deactivation. The message used real government terminology around the FMCSA biennial MCS-150 update, which carriers are genuinely required to complete every two years. The article states that this update can be completed for free at the official FMCSA portal, while the email offered paid two-year, four-year, and lifetime registration tiers.

The sender was not the FMCSA but dotregistrationsfirm[.]com, a domain registered through GoDaddy in August 2023 that styled itself as a “DOT Registrations Firm.” The email footer included a disclaimer saying the company was not the Department of Transportation, the FMCSA, or any government agency, but the article says the subject line, branding, and urgency created a government-like impression. The article frames the message as brand impersonation, payment fraud, and regulatory impersonation that relied on a real public identifier and a real compliance requirement.

Technical review found that the message was sent through a marketing platform and relayed through a security gateway before reaching the carrier’s Microsoft 365 tenant. SPF passed, but DMARC for the visible sender domain was set to p=none, DKIM verified at one hop and failed at the final receiver, and wrapped links resolved to a host different from the sender brand. The article says behavioral analysis flagged the mismatched link behavior, weak authentication enforcement, manufactured urgency, and payment request before any payment was made.

  • A real USDOT number should not be treated as proof of legitimacy because the article notes that these identifiers are publicly available in SAFER records.
  • The most effective verification step for carriers is to ignore the email’s links and go directly to the official FMCSA or SAFER site, since the MCS-150 update is free there.
  • A footer disclaimer saying the sender is not a government agency can function as legal cover while the subject line, branding, and urgency still create a government-like impression.
  • Messages can pass some authentication checks and still be risky, as shown by SPF passing while DMARC was only set to monitoring and DKIM was inconsistent across the relay path.
  • The article emphasizes that link behavior can reveal deception even when the message has no malware or credential-harvesting page, because the email showed one sender brand while its assets and unsubscribe links resolved to a different host.

In plain words

SpecterOps created ProxyWatch, a test tool meant to spot when attackers use a hacked computer as a hidden pass-through point to reach other systems without placing their tools on that computer. This matters because attackers and red teams use this method to avoid common security checks, and many organizations have trouble detecting it reliably. The people affected are defenders and organizations whose internal computers could be abused this way, because the activity can help attackers move through a network, run actions against important systems, or steal data while blending in with normal connections.

Summary
SpecterOps released ProxyWatch, a proof-of-concept tool that detects SOCKS proxy pivots, C2 sessions, and beaconing by analyzing endpoint behavior rather than relying on static indicators or process-port baselines. The key takeaway is that proxy-based attacker activity can be detected more reliably by profiling how processes communicate and relay traffic.

SpecterOps highlighted ProxyWatch, a proof-of-concept tool for detecting SOCKS proxies and other proxy pivoting methods through behavior-based detection. The article explains that adversaries use SOCKS proxy tunnels to pivot within environments and execute actions against compromised systems without bringing tools to the system. It notes that defenders often lack reliable guidance for detecting this behavior and may fall back to static indicators or process-port baselines.

ProxyWatch collects endpoint telemetry on Linux and Windows, including network, user, and process context, and builds process profiles through a scoring engine. Its rule engine includes 83 behavioral signals such as raw socket usage, loopback address usage, periodic callback cadence, measured jitter, writable paths, uncommon traffic destinations, named pipe C2 patterns, and parent-child tunnel inheritance. The tool assigns process roles such as C2 session, SOCKS proxy pivot, and beaconing behavior, and also runs a local machine learning model trained against the rule engine’s output.

The article demonstrates ProxyWatch detecting a Sliver Beacon SOCKS tunnel, identifying a Sliver C2 beacon callback pattern, collecting host-user-process-endpoint relationships through ProxyHound, and probing egress paths through Contour. It emphasizes that proxied execution can reduce disk presence and avoid detections based on process spawning because the attacker’s tools remain on the attacker system. At the same time, it notes that detecting the target activity itself, such as registry run key modification, can still reveal the technique being performed.

  • Proxied execution can evade detections built around process creation because the attacker’s tools run on the attacker’s machine while the compromised host only relays network traffic.
  • Detecting the action performed against the target, such as a registry run key modification, may succeed even when the proxied execution method itself is missed.
  • Process-port baselines for detecting proxy activity are difficult to maintain because legitimate and malicious use of ports such as Kerberos, LDAP, and Windows RPC can vary widely across environments.
  • ProxyWatch’s rule engine and local machine learning model are designed to work together, with rules providing immediate detections and the model taking over role assignment only after it reaches agreement with the rules.
  • Egress testing in ProxyWatch’s Contour component feeds results back into the classifier, so confirmed outbound paths in a specific network can influence later detection scoring.
Key Points
  • 01Adversaries use SOCKS proxy tunnels to pivot within environments and execute code against compromised systems without bringing tools to those systems.
  • 02SpecterOps created ProxyWatch as a proof-of-concept tool to detect SOCKS proxies and other pivoting methods through behavior-based detection.
  • 03ProxyWatch collects endpoint telemetry on Linux and Windows, including network, user, and process context, then scores processes using behavioral signals to assign roles such as C2 session, SOCKS proxy pivot, or beaconing behavior.
  • 04ProxyWatch includes a local machine learning model that reads 122 features per process and trains against the rule engine’s output while the rules provide detections from day one.
  • 05The article shows ProxyWatch detecting a Sliver Beacon SOCKS tunnel, a Sliver C2 beacon callback pattern, BloodHound-style relationship collection through ProxyHound, and egress paths through Contour.

This matters because the unit has played a role in major real-world operations, including the Stuxnet weapon used against Iran’s nuclear program, and some of its stolen techniques were later tied to damaging global incidents like WannaCry.

Summary
The NSA has renamed its elite offensive cyber unit back to Tailored Access Operations as part of a leadership-driven reorganization meant to speed and strengthen operations against digital threats from countries like China and Russia. The move revives a storied unit known for custom hacking tools, Stuxnet, and links to the leaked EternalBlue exploit later used in WannaCry.

The National Security Agency has changed the name of its Office of Computer Network Operations back to Tailored Access Operations, or TAO. The change is part of a reorganization by NSA’s new leadership aimed at making the agency more adept at facing evolving digital threats from China, Russia, and others. The move reverses parts of the NSA21 reshuffle launched in 2016, which had moved offensive operations and intelligence collection into broader directorates rather than keeping TAO as a standalone office.

The article says NSA Deputy Director Tim Kosiba, who previously worked in TAO, spearheaded the latest change. A former agency employee said NSA21 was not viewed as useful and said the earlier reshuffle split apart developers and operators. Other former NSA personnel believe bringing those sides back together under one roof, with TAO expected to open its own building at Fort Meade next month, will speed up operations and boost creativity.

TAO creates and deploys custom software tools to penetrate foreign computer networks for espionage purposes, including implants and other software-based methods. The unit helped craft Stuxnet, the cyber weapon used to sabotage Iran’s nuclear program. It also drew public attention after the Shadow Brokers advertised stolen hacking techniques, and the article notes that Russia and North Korea were believed to have used pilfered tools in major global cyberattacks, including the 2017 WannaCry ransomware outbreak using EternalBlue.

  • The rebrand is not just cosmetic because TAO is expected to move into its own building at Fort Meade next month, physically concentrating personnel under one roof.

  • NSA leadership is explicitly using TAO’s historical reputation and internal identity as a tool to drive future mission performance.

In plain words

Microsoft says it will remove OWA Light, an older simplified web version of Outlook for Exchange Server, in a future update estimated for August 2026. People using on-premises Exchange Server will no longer be able to choose or be sent to this older email view and should use the modern Outlook on the web instead. Microsoft says the change matters because today’s browsers and networks have improved, and removing the old option reduces legacy parts it must maintain.

Summary
Microsoft plans to disable and remove the legacy OWA Light client from on-premises Exchange Server in an upcoming update, likely in August 2026. Users will need to use the modern Outlook on the web experience, while admins can proactively block OWA Light now via Exchange PowerShell settings.

Microsoft announced plans to disable and remove OWA Light, the lightweight version of the Outlook Web App email client, in a future Exchange Server update. The Exchange Team said OWA Light was once important for compatibility, but that the full Outlook on the web experience is now where Microsoft plans to focus. Microsoft said retiring OWA Light will reduce legacy surface area, simplify engineering work, and help it continue improving the experience customers use every day.

OWA Light was introduced roughly two decades ago as an alternative to OWA Premium for systems that did not have Internet Explorer 6 or later installed or that ran older web browsers. Microsoft said at the time that OWA Light offered a cleaner look, faster logon times on low-bandwidth Internet connections, and support for locked-down browser modes such as kiosks. The article notes that OWA Light has fewer features than the standard version, including no weekly or monthly calendar views, no access to shared mailboxes or shared calendars, no import or export of messages or contacts, and no ability to create or modify tasks or notes.

Microsoft deprecated OWA Light as of August 19, 2024, and said the experience will likely be removed from on-premises Exchange Server in an upcoming update estimated for August 2026. After the change, users will no longer be able to choose or be redirected to OWA Light and should use the modern Outlook on the web experience instead. Administrators can block OWA Light immediately with Set-OwaMailboxPolicy -OwaLightEnabled $false and disable the OWA Light selection menu on the logon page with Set-OwaVirtualDirectory -LogonPageLightSelectionEnabled $false.

  • Organizations do not need to wait for the future Exchange Server update to remove OWA Light access, because Microsoft provides PowerShell commands to block it now and hide the Light option from the logon page.
  • The retirement affects only the legacy OWA Light experience, not Outlook on the web as a whole, so users are being directed to the modern full web experience rather than losing browser-based email access.
  • Microsoft frames the change partly as a security and maintenance reduction, saying removal will reduce legacy surface area and simplify ongoing engineering work.
  • OWA Light’s original purpose has largely diminished because Microsoft says modern browsers are more capable and consistent, network conditions have improved for many customers, and the security landscape has changed significantly.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft announced plans to disable and remove OWA Light from Exchange Server in an upcoming update estimated for August 2026.
  • 02OWA Light was introduced roughly two decades ago as a simplified alternative for systems without Internet Explorer 6 or later, older browsers, low-bandwidth connections, or locked-down browser modes such as kiosks.
  • 03Microsoft said retiring OWA Light will reduce legacy surface area, simplify engineering work, and allow it to focus on the full Outlook on the web experience.
  • 04After the change is introduced, users will no longer be able to choose or be redirected to OWA Light and should use the modern Outlook on the web experience instead.
  • 05Admins can block OWA Light immediately with Set-OwaMailboxPolicy -OwaLightEnabled $false and remove the light selection menu on the logon page with Set-OwaVirtualDirectory -LogonPageLightSelectionEnabled $false.

In plain words

Cloudflare explains that the security methods used for decades to prove identities online could be broken by powerful future quantum computers, and that the replacement methods available today are bigger and less convenient. Cloudflare says it cannot wait for better replacements that are still being studied, because those are unlikely to be widely usable until the 2030s, while Cloudflare wants to be fully protected by 2029. This affects major Internet systems such as secure website connections and certificates, and the broader risk is that attackers could eventually bypass trust systems if the move to quantum-safe protections starts too late.

Summary
Cloudflare argues organizations cannot wait for newer, smaller post-quantum signature algorithms because they likely will not be widely deployable until the 2030s. The practical path is to begin migrating now with ML-DSA despite its drawbacks, while continuing research into better alternatives for future upgrades.

Cloudflare argues that organizations cannot wait for better post-quantum signature algorithms before migrating away from RSA and ECC, because sufficiently advanced quantum computers would be able to break those older systems. The article says ML-KEM encryption and ML-DSA signatures were standardized by NIST in 2024 after an eight-year competition, and Cloudflare is targeting 2029 to become fully post-quantum secure. It notes that much of Cloudflare’s traffic already uses ML-KEM encryption, but authentication systems still need post-quantum signatures.

The article compares current and candidate post-quantum signature schemes, including ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, FN-DSA, SQIsign, UOV, MAYO, SNOVA, HAWK, FAEST, MQOM, and SDitH. It says there is no single post-quantum “all-star” equivalent to elliptic-curve signatures: some schemes have small signatures but slow signing, huge public keys, difficult secure implementations, or newer security assumptions. ML-DSA is described as the available general-purpose option today, even though it has larger sizes and fewer tricks than RSA and ECC.

Cloudflare says the newer signature algorithms will not be ready in time for the first post-quantum transition, with broad availability for many candidates expected in the 2030s. The article argues that migration must start now because large systems need transition periods, and supporting both old and new signatures can create downgrade risks. It also says continued NIST work remains important because smaller future signatures and related techniques may help systems that cannot easily absorb ML-DSA’s costs and may support tools such as anonymous credentials.

  • The article warns that meeting a 2035 post-quantum deadline by deploying signatures in 2034 would still be insufficient, because large systems need a long period supporting both old and new signatures, which can create downgrade risks.
  • FN-DSA’s main weakness is not verification but signing: the article says verification is straightforward, while secure signing is difficult because different floating-point implementations can behave differently and may affect testability and side-channel safety.
  • Some post-quantum signature schemes are useful even if they are not ready for the first migration, because their underlying methods can support other hard-to-replace tools such as anonymous credentials and blind signatures.
  • The article says there is no single post-quantum signature algorithm that replaces elliptic-curve signatures across all important measures, so different systems may need different trade-offs between signature size, public key size, speed, and implementation risk.
  • Cloudflare argues that NIST’s continued signature competition is still a good use of resources even though the candidates will arrive too late for the first migration, because smaller future signatures could remove costly compensating controls in systems that cannot efficiently use ML-DSA.
Key Points
  • 01Cloudflare says RSA and ECC are vulnerable to sufficiently advanced quantum computers, and it is targeting 2029 to become fully post-quantum secure.
  • 02The article argues that newer post-quantum signature algorithms will not be ready in time for the first transition, so ML-DSA must be used despite larger sizes and reduced flexibility compared with RSA and ECC.
  • 03NIST advanced nine post-quantum signature schemes to the third round of its signatures on-ramp, while a draft standard for FN-DSA is expected imminently.
  • 04The article says FN-DSA has smaller keys and signatures than ML-DSA but is difficult to implement securely for signing because of issues involving floating-point arithmetic and side-channel safety.
  • 05Cloudflare argues continued work on new signature schemes remains important because some systems cannot easily absorb ML-DSA’s size costs and because the research may help enable other post-quantum tools such as anonymous credentials.

In plain words

The article says many groups are announcing places to collect secret reports about weaknesses in open source software, but the author argues that collecting reports is not enough. What matters is whether those reports quickly become fixed, tested software that people and companies can actually use. This affects anyone whose apps rely on shared open source code, because a flaw in a small hidden piece can put the whole app at risk. The broader stakes are that attackers may use weaknesses before fixes are public, so the organizations handling these reports need to move fast and eventually help make the underlying software harder to break in the first place.

Summary
The article argues that the new wave of open source vulnerability clearinghouses only matters if they can rapidly turn private findings into rebuilt, tested, signed, and upstreamed fixes. The real measure of success is throughput and reach, not how many vulnerabilities a clearinghouse holds.

The article argues that the recent wave of open source vulnerability clearinghouse announcements is a response to a real shift, but that the clearinghouse itself is not the most important part. Chainguard says its Athena clearinghouse was already operating before its announcement, taking private findings and shipping fixes because customers asked for it. The author says these clearinghouses are mainly pools of pre-disclosure vulnerability data, while the real value is turning findings into rebuilt, tested, signed fixes that users can actually consume.

The article says the flood of private findings is a byproduct of AI models being tested against running applications, where they find exploitable flaws across both first-party code and open source dependencies. Because applications depend heavily on open source code, flaws in obscure dependencies can still affect the whole running process. The author argues that bigger, faster clearinghouses are more useful than small or slow ones because many findings land in the same widely used libraries, and because a backlog of embargoed findings becomes a leak surface.

The article’s main test for any clearinghouse is whether it can measure and improve throughput and reach: median time from finding to rebuilt, tested, signed fix; the fraction handled without human intervention; and how many fixes land upstream rather than only reaching the vendor’s own customers. Chainguard says Athena has taken in more than twenty thousand findings and shipped over two thousand patches across five hundred projects, but says the more important number is how many fixes are accepted upstream. The author concludes that clearinghouses are a temporary safety net, while the long-term goal should be secure-by-design open source software that makes whole classes of attacks impossible.

  • The article frames a growing clearinghouse backlog as a warning sign rather than a success metric, because findings waiting under embargo are the current leak surface.
  • The author argues that smaller clearinghouses are not necessarily safer, because a slow operator can accumulate more dangerous in-flight findings than a larger operator with faster fix throughput.
  • The article says public disclosure can increase risk because a published fix acts as a map to the bug, and Chainguard claims it has seen an advisory become a working exploit in under an hour.
  • The author predicts that the sustainable model is not one universal clearinghouse or many fragmented ones, but a few large clearinghouses that can coordinate with each other and reach enough partners to act quickly.
  • The article’s proposed vendor test is actionable: ask for median time from finding to rebuilt, tested, signed fix, the fraction handled without humans, and the share of fixes accepted upstream rather than only delivered to that vendor’s customers.

In plain words

The article says AI tools inside companies can quietly gain access to more systems over time, such as code, tickets, documents, and data stores, until no one knows exactly what they can reach. This matters because attackers have already taken over company AI agents and used their approved access to move quickly through defense, energy, and technology targets, and a Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw showed how one crafted email could pull data from OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams. Companies using these AI agents are affected, and the broader risk is that sensitive business data can be exposed through access that seemed harmless when it was added piece by piece.

Summary
AI agents are accumulating permissions through integrations and inherited access faster than traditional reviews can track, creating “authority drift” that attackers can exploit using the agents’ own legitimate access. Organizations need live visibility and real-time enforcement of agent permissions rather than relying on static approval records or periodic reviews.

The article discusses “authority drift,” defined as the expansion of an AI agent’s permission footprint beyond what was originally approved until nobody can account for everything it can reach. It describes a case where a coding agent started with recorded read access to a code repository but later gained connections to a ticketing system, a documentation tool, and a data store. The article argues that this creates a gap between what security teams think an agent can do and what it can actually do.

The article says authority drift does not behave like traditional overprovisioning because AI agent permissions can change faster than quarterly access reviews can catch. It identifies three drivers of growth: inherited access from connected systems, new integrations added by developers, and broad access granted for convenience. It also cites September 2025 incidents where state-sponsored attackers hijacked enterprise AI agent instances across 30 defense, energy, and technology targets, and CVE-2025-32711, a Microsoft 365 Copilot zero-click prompt injection that extracted data from OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams.

The article’s main significance is that organizations often lack a current map of what each AI agent can reach, while agent deployment is increasing across enterprise applications. It says static inventories from deployment quickly become outdated when integrations or data stores change. The article recommends a live map of agent access, restrictions to fixed tools or models, and an enforcement point that can scope access without waiting for the next scheduled review.

  • Traditional quarterly access reviews are poorly matched to AI agents because the article says an agent’s permissions can expand in weeks rather than years.
  • The article highlights that individually reasonable access decisions by separate teams can combine into an overall permission footprint that no single team approved or understands.
  • The article argues that visibility alone is insufficient because a live access map and tool restrictions only produce reports unless there is an enforcement point that can act before the next scheduled review.
  • The article warns that continuous monitoring can fail operationally if every integration change triggers an alert, because overstretched security teams may tune out the noise within a quarter.
  • The article frames the most useful governance question as procedural rather than static: who last checked what an agent can reach, and when.
Key Points

  • 02The article says AI agent access grows through inherited permissions from connected systems, new integrations added to solve immediate problems, and broad access granted for convenience.
  • 03In September 2025, state-sponsored attackers hijacked enterprise AI agent instances across 30 targets in defense, energy, and technology, using the agents’ accumulated access to move laterally in minutes.
  • 04CVE-2025-32711 was described as a zero-click prompt injection in Microsoft 365 Copilot that used a crafted email to extract data from OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams through a trusted Microsoft domain.
  • 05The article argues that organizations need a live map of each agent’s access, restrictions to a fixed set of tools or models, and an enforcement point that can scope access without waiting for the next scheduled review.
